title: Checkpoint: where a week stands after a day of taking it apart
lede: This release closes what the last four left open, and marks the place. A week of an online coding course now costs $0.53 to write and check where it cost $0.97 this morning, the reading and fixing of a page take about a minute where they took four, and pages read blind by a reviewer score what they did or a little better. What is still wrong is listed at the end.

sections.heading: The reader was policing rules meant for the writer
sections.body: The model that reads a page is told about the course as the writer is, and with it came the writer’s own instructions: how deadlines are to be worded, what is written separately, who lectures. It held pages to them. Nearly half of what it listed was no fault of the page, and some of its ready-made changes wrote a deadline, a grading rule or a demand for one version of Python into a page that had none. It is now told those instructions are not its to enforce. What it lists that is no fault fell from 47 in a hundred to 37, and it lists a third fewer things. On twelve pages with 28 known faults it found 25, where it had found 27 before; so we judged the finished pages rather than the reading: six weeks each way, read blind, 7.75 of 10 against 7.83, two stopping faults against three, nine false statements against eleven.

image.alt: Four bars: what one week of an online coding course cost to write and check. Release 0.0.15, $0.97. Release 0.0.16, $0.68, the page written without thinking itself to a stop. Release 0.0.18, $0.58, the reading at lower effort. Release 0.0.19, $0.53, the reader no longer polices the writer’s rules

sections.heading: Rules that were read out to students
sections.body: Several things Folio tells the writer were turning up on the page as if students needed them: “every component is scored by points or rubric levels, not complete or incomplete”, “nothing is handed out or said aloud”, and parts whose only content was “open the separately posted step”. Each came from an instruction worded so that it asked to be repeated. They are reworded, and in the last runs on five courses none of them appears.

sections.heading: Things that did not agree with each other
sections.body: A page gave a small ungraded step “by Sunday” that the step’s own text set five weeks on: the page is now told each piece’s real deadline. A version check showed the Python that Folio runs code on, above a sentence saying it should print the course’s: such a cell never shows Folio’s versions now, and the setup makes one environment with exactly the versions the course names. An assignment gave other measurements to an object the page had students build under the same name: a new item now has a name of its own. A picture went on being asked to show a number the code no longer printed. And a variable’s name was reused for a function further down, which broke the notebook when run again from the top.

sections.heading: The answer check, measured again
sections.body: After the four repairs of 0.0.16, on the same 113 questions: it finds six of nine real errors where it found five, and blames two of 64 sound questions where it blamed five, for half the money. The measurement also showed that one of the repairs had let an error through, by matching a result of 1.459 to a stray “1” further along the line; that is mended in this release and has a test.

sections.heading: Still wrong
sections.body: A troubleshooting note still sometimes names a cause that does not give the symptom it is listed under; asking the writer for true ones was not enough, and the real answer is to run them. The reader still proposes a change that should not be made about seven times in a hundred. A fix sometimes leaves the corrected sentence beside the one it corrects. The teacher’s summary of what students’ work holds can go stale when a page is mended. The last checks in this release were made with command-line tools, which show what a page says but not what it costs. No teacher has yet read any of these pages: every score here is another model’s.

title: A week’s page is read and put right in half the time, with fewer notes left for you
lede: After a week’s page is written, a second model reads it as a student would and the writer puts right what it finds. That reading and fixing had become more than half of what a week costs. We took it apart, call by call and note by note, and most of what we changed is a fault removed.

sections.heading: What we found in the notes
sections.body: We had twelve first readings checked one by one. Every reading found every fault that mattered, 28 in all. But between a third and a half of what each reading listed was no fault, and the same kinds came back: a checklist’s minutes added up a hundred too many; a deadline or a grading rule written into a page that had never given one; “your version may differ a little” turned into a demand. Small changes of that kind were being made to pages without anyone asking. The reader is now told what is not its to list, and the false totals are gone: none in twelve readings where there had been five.

image.alt: Three figures, each the mean of six weeks. What the reading and the fixes cost: $0.23, where it was $0.34. How long they take: 2 minutes, where it was 4. Notes left for the teacher to settle in a week: 0.3, where it was 1.5

sections.heading: Faults of ours that sent pages back
sections.body: Folio’s own check asked every notebook week for a screenshot of a cell and a recording of it being run, though the cell’s real output is already on the page: eleven weeks of twelve were sent to be mended for pictures a teacher would then have had to make. It no longer asks. A rule about work that depends on a classmate’s was written so that it was pasted, word for word and unreadable, into the checklists of weeks with no such work; it is rewritten. A note that a sentence quoted an old number was sent to the writer even after the reader had already corrected the sentence. A checklist item was left out of the week’s hours if it so much as mentioned the word optional, which put some weeks forty minutes under what they asked. And the teacher’s list of things to check quoted numbers from before the code was run; those entries now go when the run replaces the numbers.

sections.heading: What we tried and did not take
sections.body: The reader now reads at a lower effort, since it no longer has to run the page’s code in its head: it found the same 28 faults, in under half the time. We tried the same economy on the writer’s fixes, and it failed: twelve fixes made without thinking first were set beside the twelve made with it, blind, and lost ten times, once by inventing the output of code that had been run. Fixes think as they did.

sections.heading: The result
sections.body: A week of an online coding course costs about $0.58 to write, where it was $0.68, and is ready about two minutes sooner. Six weeks written each way were read blind: 7.7 of 10 against 7.3, the gain in sentences that should never have been on the page. Two of the six new pages had a fault that would stop a student, both of kinds seen before these changes; one, a version check that showed Folio’s Python and not the course’s, has a fix in this release that is not yet measured.

title: Claude is now told what each part of its answer is for
lede: Looking for what else a week’s page costs, we found something that cost nothing and was simply broken: most of the notes that tell the model what each field of its answer is for were never sent to it. They are now, and pages come out better formed for the same money.

sections.heading: What was lost on the way
sections.body: Folio holds a model to a shape: a page has parts, a part has blocks, a block has a kind, a title, a picture to ask for. Beside most fields is a line saying what belongs there. For Claude, the library that sends the shape dropped that line from every field that has a default or is used twice: 116 of 160, among them what a callout’s title is, what a picture must give a student who cannot see it, and nearly everything about the notes a teacher gets with a week. The model worked from the long instructions alone. Other providers’ models were not affected.

image.alt: Two bars. As it was, 44 of the 160 descriptions written in Folio’s shapes reached Claude. Now all 160 do. Among those that never arrived: what a callout’s title is, what a picture gives a student who cannot see it, who to contact this week and what to say

sections.heading: What changes on the page
sections.body: Six weeks written each way were read blind, and the reader, asked whether the pages fell into two kinds, sorted all twelve correctly. With the descriptions, callouts have titles, the teacher’s notes name this week’s variables and say what to write to a student who has not started, and more pictures are asked for: 7.9 of 10 against 7.5, the difference in form and in the teacher’s notes, not in what is taught. Four lessons taught in a room, read the same way, came out level. The cost is the same.

sections.heading: What we tried and did not take
sections.body: A fifth of what a week’s page costs is empty fields: every block writes ten, and seven are usually blank. Let the model leave them out and it does; but five pages of six then came back as a handful of blocks and the word “Placeholder”. They stay. What is left of a page’s cost is the page.

sections.heading: Still wrong
sections.body: The teacher’s list of things to check in a week with code can quote numbers from before the code was run, which differ from those on the page. The page itself is put right; that list is not yet.

title: A week of an online coding course costs about a third less to write
lede: We traced every call Folio makes for a week of a course and found that a quarter of the money bought nothing: pages written and thrown away. That is gone, and the pages that come out were judged no worse.

sections.heading: Where the money went
sections.body: Before writing a week that teaches code, the model thought at length, working out by hand what every cell would print. In four runs of six it thought until its answer was full, wrote nothing, and was asked again; the second time it thought little and wrote a good page. The page is now written straight away, at the same care as before, and Folio runs the code to learn what it prints, as it has since 0.0.13. A page whose optional reading took no time was also being written again whole for that alone; it no longer is, and an optional item with no time shows none.

image.alt: Two bars. As it was, a week cost $0.97, of which $0.23 was written and thrown away and $0.22 the week’s page. Now it costs $0.68: the page $0.13, putting right what the review found $0.15, the review $0.14, the rest $0.17

sections.heading: How we know the pages are no worse
sections.body: Six weeks written each way, from three courses, were read blind by a reviewer who did not know which was which, as an instructor would before releasing them: 8.1 of 10 for the new way and 7.9 for the old, one page with a fault that would stop a student on each side. A cheaper setting we tried first, which saved a little more, scored 6.9 with four such faults in a reading where the old way scored 8.3, and we did not take it. One thing is not as good: a first draft now draws more notes from its review (about seventeen where there were eleven), so the review and the fixes cost a little more and a teacher is left a note more often. It is counted in the figure above.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: A fix now gives only the blocks that change; it used to type whole parts again, half of them untouched. The answer check costs half what it did for each question, and four faults of its own are mended: it took 2 for 3, could miss an error it had found twice when the two findings quoted the text differently, let a form narrow the rounding rule, and blamed a question for a form left empty. A week with no code, or a lesson taught in a room, costs about what it did; a lesson with a quiz to check, a little less.

sections.heading: What this is measured on
sections.body: Three courses in Python, first weeks, with Folio credits (Claude Sonnet 5.5), and one week of a Unity course, which came out better the new way in its one comparison. With your own key and another model, pages are written as before.

title: A fault of ours in online courses, and four things teachers asked for
lede: First, a correction. For some hours after the last release, a course taught online could not be written with a paid model, and the answer check added two releases ago was not really checking. Both are fixed. Then: slides with tables and charts, a copy of a handout for students still learning English, standards codes on lessons, and slips and cards that print as slips and cards.

sections.heading: What went wrong, and what we changed so it does not again
sections.body: The last release let a week’s page hold tables and notes as real content. The way that was described to the model made the request larger than the model’s provider accepts, and every weekly page of an online course was refused; lessons taught in a room were not affected. Separately, the check that computes answers was asking the model for a form in a way that the paid models answered with an empty one, so it had been passing everything without computing anything. We did not see either because our test runs used a route that does not hold the model to the shape of its answer. Both are fixed, and before each release every such shape is now sent to the provider itself. Run for real on a statistics week, the check computed five of seven answers.

sections.heading: Slides can hold a table or a chart
sections.body: A deck was bullets and nothing else. Where a lesson compares things under the same headings, the slide is now a table; where it compares numbers or follows them over time, a chart drawn from those numbers, bars or a line. In PowerPoint the table is a real table and the chart a real chart, so you can restyle either or change a value there; in Folio you change the numbers under the slide and the chart is drawn again. Numbers made up to show a shape are marked as an illustration on the slide. Diagrams and drawings are not made yet.

image.alt: A slide with a bar chart of two bars, 8 and 2, labelled in milligrams of starch and marked as an illustration, with one question under it

sections.heading: A copy of a handout with language supports
sections.body: About six teachers in ten say they lack materials for students still learning English. Under each handout you can now ask for a copy with supports: the same task, questions and answers, with shorter instructions, a word bank, one worked example and sentence starters. Nothing is made easier or taken out, and nothing on the student’s sheet says it is a different version. It is a draft for you to read: of the first nine we had judged, five could be printed as they were and four needed a line or two changed, usually a word’s meaning.

sections.heading: Standards on the lessons that serve them
sections.body: When your brief or your files name standards by their codes, each lesson now says which it serves, in the plan and in what you export. Folio keeps only codes you gave it and never adds one.

sections.heading: Slips and cards print as slips and cards
sections.body: An exit ticket took a page to itself, and cards came as a list that could not be cut apart. In a document, slips now come three to a page with a line to cut along, and cards one to a cell of a grid.

title: The sheets a lesson hands out are written, not just named
lede: Four changes, each made because teachers say it is where generated lessons fall short: materials a plan names and does not include, pictures left for the teacher to make, quizzes that will not go into the LMS, and lessons that only ask students to repeat what they were shown.

sections.heading: Handouts, written in full
sections.body: A plan would say “hand out the exit ticket” or “students sort the cards”, and that was all there was of the ticket and the cards. Counted over six of Folio’s own courses, a lesson needed about thirteen things made and nearly half were left to you. For a lesson taught in a room, Folio now writes every sheet the plan puts in students’ hands: worksheets, exit tickets, organizers, cards, short texts, each from the plan’s own numbers and examples, with room to answer sized to the question. The answers stand beside the sheet for you and never on it. Sheets are edited under the plan and exported with it, each on its own page. A reviewer who worked all 94 answers on the first twenty sheets by hand found none wrong; nine sheets could be printed as they were, eight needed a small fix and three were not usable, mostly for their layout.

image.alt: A worksheet under a lesson plan: ratio tables with empty cells to fill in, room to write under each, and an answer key for the teacher below the sheet

sections.heading: What the course wrote is shown, not described
sections.body: On an online page, seven picture places in ten asked for a picture of something the page had itself written: your notes as they should now stand, a model email, a filled-in table. You were left to make each by hand from its description. The page now holds the thing itself: real text and real tables, edited where they stand, read aloud properly, and real tables in a Word file. One that shows what students are about to write stays closed until they open it to compare. On the first two courses written this way, a three-week course in technical writing went from about fourteen pictures for you to make to none; in psychology, the ten left are real screens and drawings. Read one by one, 41 of 54 could be used as they were and none was unusable.

image.alt: A page of notes shown as a table on the course page, with a note on one column and a button to hide it again

sections.heading: Quizzes that go into Canvas
sections.body: The quiz bank left Folio as a spreadsheet, to be typed into the LMS again. It can now leave as a package Canvas imports (Settings, Import Course Content, QTI .zip file): one quiz for each lesson, with its key. Canvas marks the questions that have one right choice and the numeric ones; a short answer becomes a question you read, with the model answer as its comment. It imports as Classic Quizzes, the kind teachers report importing reliably. We have checked that the package is well formed and follows the format; we have not yet imported one into a real Canvas course, so please tell us if yours does not come in cleanly.

sections.heading: One task beyond practice, and a quiz as hard as the lesson
sections.body: We measured 40 of Folio’s lessons the way a published study measured machine-written plans. Where that study found 45 activities in 100 asking students only to recall, Folio’s had 9. But in mathematics and chemistry no lesson went beyond practising the method just shown, the teacher explained for up to 28 minutes at a stretch, and the quiz was shallower than the lesson. A plan now holds one task a step beyond practice, at the students’ level (find and fix the mistake, choose between two ways and say why), in place of some of the practice; long explanation is broken by something every student does; and a quiz asks at least once for the hardest thing the lesson did. Measured again on nine lessons: none stops at practice, the longest stretch of explanation is 16 minutes, and students are active for 62 minutes in 100, up from 38.

sections.heading: You can see which answers were checked
sections.body: A quiz question whose key Folio computed, and found to hold, now says so under it. Change the question and the mark goes, since what was checked is no longer what is there.

title: Folio runs the code it writes
lede: The Python on a week’s page is now run before you see the page, and the page shows what the code really prints. Answers that can be worked out are worked out, and the ones that don’t hold are marked for you.

sections.heading: The page shows what the code prints
sections.body: In an online course taught in a notebook, Folio wrote each cell and, under it, what it expected the cell to print. Nothing had run. Now every cell of a week is run in order, in a fresh notebook, and the output on the page is what came out: in place of what was written, or under a cell that had none. A chart a cell draws is placed under the cell. A cell that fails is sent back to be corrected with its real error, and so is a sentence that quotes a number the code does not print; what could not be put right is noted for you. Each output says what ran it. One kind of cell is left as written: one that asks the computer about itself, such as which version of pandas is installed, since the answer is about your students’ computers, not Folio’s.

image.alt: Before, the output under a cell was what the writer expected, here a wrong 5; now it is what the code printed when Folio ran it, 6, marked as run on Python 3.14

sections.heading: Answers that can be computed are
sections.body: The mistakes in a generated course were not where we looked for them. In four courses, the code on the pages was right, but 8 of 49 quiz questions and answer keys had a wrong key or a wrong explanation, and no reading had caught one. For any question or answer key with code or numbers in it, Folio now builds the item’s data, computes what the item claims, and compares the result with the words in the item. What fails twice is marked on the item, with the value it states and the value computed. Folio never changes a key by itself: you decide. On the first two courses written this way it marked three real mistakes in 43 items, among them the one pictured, and one item that was right; what caused that false alarm is fixed.

image.alt: An answer key that gives a chi-square statistic of 0.581, with a note under it: Folio ran this and it did not hold; computed from the counts, it is 0.867

sections.heading: Where the code runs, and what it can reach
sections.body: The code runs in your own browser, so it costs you nothing and needs no account. It is shut in a frame that has none of Folio’s storage and is allowed no connection of any kind: it cannot read your courses or your keys, and it cannot send anything anywhere. A cell that runs too long, or takes too much memory, is stopped. The first time a course needs it, your browser fetches Python and its libraries (about 6 MB, or about 25 MB with pandas and Matplotlib) and keeps them. Folio’s Python is 3.14, with pandas 3.0, NumPy 2.4, Matplotlib 3.10, SciPy 1.18, statsmodels 0.14 and scikit-learn 1.8; a course you write for older versions is still written for yours, and its outputs say which version ran them. On a phone the code is not run, and the page is kept as written.

image.alt: Folio’s page holds your courses, account and keys; the runner is a frame with a Python in it; code goes in, text and pictures come out, and nothing else passes

sections.heading: A notebook of each week
sections.body: When you export a course as a zip, each week that has Python now comes with a Jupyter notebook: the week’s words as text and its code as cells, in order, so a student can run the week instead of typing it out. The teacher’s copy also shows what each cell printed.

sections.heading: Two faults found on the way
sections.body: Checking answers by running them showed that code of more than one line, inside a quiz choice or an answer, had its straight quotes turned into curly ones with the prose around it, and would not run when copied; such code is now left exactly as written. And a security review of this work found that a backup file made by hand could give a file a type the browser would run as a page; a file kept with a course is now shown only as a picture or a video, and anything else is a download. That fix went out earlier today.

title: Work that waits on a classmate is due after theirs
lede: Three faults in how a course is put together, each found by reading a whole course through, and one plain page of what to know before you rely on Folio.

sections.heading: A review is due after the draft it reviews
sections.body: In an online course with peer review, the draft and the reviews of it were both due on Sunday night, so there was nothing to review until the hour the review was due. Work that needs a classmate’s work to exist now comes after it: what classmates will work on is posted by Thursday, and the work on it is due that Sunday, the same every week.

image.alt: Before, a weekly draft and the reviews of it were both due Sunday night; now the draft is posted by Thursday and the reviews are due Sunday

sections.heading: A milestone you name gets a task of its own
sections.body: When a brief named a step on the way to a larger piece, a prospectus in week 8 or a draft in week 10, Folio mentioned it in that week’s summary and wrote no task for it: no length, no contents, nothing to hand in. Each such milestone is now a task in the week you gave, and Folio no longer adds steps of its own that fall due the same day.

sections.heading: A week’s hours are estimated, not made to fit
sections.body: An online week is planned for the hours you give it, and every week came out at exactly that number, including weeks that would take a student half as long again. Each item is now timed from what it asks (reading, a first draft, steps to follow, finding a partner), work that does not fit moves to another week or becomes optional, and the second reader times each item again and says where it disagrees.

sections.heading: What to know before you rely on it
sections.body: The About page now says three things plainly: Folio writes in English for schools and universities in the United States and Canada; what it writes is a draft for you to read before you teach it; and for a course that teaches software, it needs your notes on the version your students use.

title: Your pictures on every device you sign in on
lede: The last release let you put pictures, clips and files into a page, and kept them in the browser you added them in. They now go to your account as well.

sections.heading: Added once, there everywhere
sections.body: When you are signed in, each picture, clip or file you add to a course’s pages is sent to your account after the course itself. On another device, a page that names one fetches it when you open the page, and an export or a backup made there fetches whatever it still lacks. A file can be up to 95 MB and an account can hold 2 GB; anything larger stays in the browser it was added in, and a backup file still carries it. The files are private to your account, and deleting a course or the account deletes them. Nothing changes if you do not sign in: everything stays in your browser, as before.

image.alt: A picture added on this computer is sent once to your account and fetched by your other device when you open the page

title: What a review finds is put right where it stands
lede: We listed what was wrong with how Folio writes a course, then worked through the list and wrote six courses again to see what held: a doctoral seminar, a grade 8 writing unit, and four online courses. This release is what came of it, including two faults of our own that the check-ups turned up.

sections.heading: Problems are mended, not written around
sections.body: Every lesson plan and weekly page is read a second time by another model before anything is built on it. Where that reading found problems it could not fix in a few words, Folio used to write the whole page again and keep whichever version had fewer. The new page lost the problems it was told of and brought its own, so about as many reached you as before. Now only the parts at fault are written again, and the reviewer reads them again, told what the first reading found. Over 34 weekly pages of three online courses, the first reading left 259 notes and 67 were left at the end. That is not none: a reviewer reading a page again usually finds something new, and some of what stays is yours to decide.

image.alt: Before, every part of a page was written again when a review found problems; now only the parts at fault are written again and read again. Across 34 pages, 259 notes became 67

sections.heading: Each note can be fixed, or settled, on its own
sections.body: Notes on a plan used to stand as one paragraph with one button that cleared them all. Each now has its own line, with two choices: “It’s fine”, or “Fix it”, which writes again the part the note is about and leaves the rest of the page, and its pictures, as they are. When a note turns on a choice that is yours (should two things be due the same night?), Folio says so and asks; type what you have decided and it fixes the page to match. A course with notes still on it now says how many on its card in the library, where it used to look finished.

image.alt: A lesson plan with two notes from its review, each with its own Fix it and It’s fine

sections.heading: Weeks are no longer written one at a time
sections.body: A week is written from the weeks before it, so that it uses their names and carries on their work. Each used to wait for the one before to be written, checked and corrected. A week now starts from the one before as first written, while that one is still being checked, and its own check reads the corrected version. A fourteen-week online course that took about three hours to write took about an hour and forty minutes on the same machine, with other courses being written beside it; a thirteen-meeting doctoral seminar took sixteen minutes. We then read all fourteen weeks for a project, scene, script or setting that a later week names wrongly because of this, and found none. What we did find was of another kind: a later week not allowing for what a challenge had added to a shared file. That is on our list.

sections.heading: Pictures, clips and files go into the page
sections.body: A weekly page for a software course asks for screenshots, short recordings and files, and says what each must show. Until now there was nowhere to put them. Each place now takes a file: pick it, drop it on the place, or paste a screenshot. A picture gets a caption and a description for students who cannot see it, both yours to edit. Pictures go into the Word file, everything goes into the zip in a media folder, and a backup file carries them. They are kept in this browser only for now: signing in does not yet carry them to your other devices, and the page says so where it matters.

image.alt: Two places for screenshots on a weekly page, each saying what the picture must show, with an Add picture button, and a file to attach

sections.heading: A picture can be looked at beside its step
sections.body: A review that reads a page’s words cannot see its pictures. When we followed a course by hand, the pictures were where the mistakes hid: a window from a later step, a setting cut off at the edge. “Check” shows the picture to a model together with the steps that lead to it, and lists where the two disagree, and anything in the picture that names a person or an account. We tried it on twenty pictures from that course, ten in their own places and ten swapped for another: all ten swapped ones were named. Of the ten in the right place, five came back clean and the rest with notes that were true of them, such as an outline that had been asked for and not drawn.

image.alt: A screenshot of an Inspector with a note under it: the caption speaks of a setting that the picture cuts off

sections.heading: What Folio could not check is listed for you
sections.body: When a page teaches software, the names of menus and buttons change from one version to the next, and Folio writes from what you gave it and, past that, from memory. We tested whether it could look the names up instead: a model with only the tool’s own documentation got 129 of 244 facts right that we had checked in the tool itself, 13 wrong, and had nothing on the rest. That is not good enough to state as fact, so Folio does not do it. Instead, each week’s instructor notes now list what the page states without a source of yours to go by, for you to try before the week opens; and when a brief names software without a version, Folio asks which.

sections.heading: Two faults of ours, found and fixed
sections.body: Since version 0.0.7 Folio has recorded, for each graded component, whether it is scored or graded complete or incomplete. Writing courses again for this release, we found it had marked nearly every component as complete or incomplete, a 60% seminar paper among them, and told every page so. The question it was asked could be read two ways. It is now asked in words that cannot, and believed only when your brief speaks of completion itself. If you made a course since October 4, look at the grading table on its syllabus and set each component as you mean it. The second: a week’s total hours counted optional reading and make-up work, so a nine-hour week read as ten.

sections.heading: Smaller things
sections.body: Later lessons see more of what earlier ones said: the two lessons just before are shown at length, and those further back in brief where they used to be left out. Lines added to a file after it was first written are passed on with it. A weekly task set in the same words every week is written for an online week as that week’s work, not as something handed in at the start of a class. Two different pieces of one component done in class are each written, where the second used to be a copy of the first. A test covers only what was taught before it is sat. An exit ticket in a live session has one standing place. Screenshots are asked for where steps are followed on a screen, not under every list of steps. The grading table shows how many pieces a component has and what each is worth.

title: Later weeks use the names earlier weeks gave
lede: We followed a fourteen-week course by hand, step by step, and looked at every picture in it. Most of what went wrong was not in any one page: it was between pages. This release puts what we learned into how Folio writes, so the next course does not need the same hand.

sections.heading: The files a course has written are passed on whole
sections.body: In a course that teaches software, each week builds on the files of the weeks before. A later week used to be told about them in a summary, in the summary’s own words, and the words drifted: a setting called Speed came back as “Patrol Speed”, and a game moved with A, W, S and D was given a hint about the arrow keys. A later week is now shown the files themselves, as the last week to touch each one wrote it, and takes names, settings and keys from there. We wrote weeks 12 and 13 of the same course again to check: week 13 used week 12’s script names, settings and keys as its files have them.

image.alt: Before, week 13 was told about week 12 in a summary and wrote names that did not exist; now it is shown the files and uses their names

sections.heading: No error message quoted from memory
sections.body: Pages for software courses were asked to give “the exact error text”. Where the teacher’s sources did not have it, Folio wrote one from memory, and some were wrong: a message that never appears, or a rule about which line an error is reported on that is not true. A page now quotes a message only when your sources give it. Otherwise it tells the student what to look for and to read their own.

sections.heading: A list of what is still to be made
sections.body: A weekly page asks for pictures, short recordings and files, each described for whoever makes it. Those descriptions were scattered through the page. The instructor’s copy of each week now ends with one list: every picture, recording and file still to be made, where it sits, and what it must show. Each picture is described in the state its own step leaves, before anything a later step adds, because a picture taken later shows things the student does not have yet.

sections.heading: Work typed just before leaving is kept
sections.body: As a page closes, Folio keeps a copy of anything not yet saved. In one case it threw that copy away: when an earlier save was still on its way as you left. A lesson renamed a moment before closing the tab could come back with its old name. Fixed.

sections.heading: A shorter About page
sections.body: About said who makes Folio twice and repeated the home page. It now says each thing once: what Folio is and for whom, the three steps of using it, who makes it and how to write to them.

image.alt: The About page: a headline, three numbered steps, and a card naming the maker with an email address

title: A long page is no longer thrown away for one line too many
lede: One week of a long online course failed to be written three times in a row, then passed when tried again. The cause was a limit that was stricter than it needed to be.

sections.heading: Looser limits on a weekly page
sections.body: A weekly page for an online course could have at most sixteen items on its checklist. In one fourteen-week course ten weeks had exactly sixteen, and a page that came back with seventeen was rejected whole, after minutes of writing. The limits on the checklist, the parts of a page, the vocabulary and the instructor’s lists are looser now. What Folio asks for has not changed: the page it aims at is the same length as before.

image.alt: Before, a seventeenth checklist item threw the whole page away; now the page is kept

title: One way to say how work is graded
lede: A review of a whole fourteen-week course found the same piece of work described two ways: scored by its rubric on one page, complete or incomplete on three others. Each page had been written well and none agreed. This release makes how work is graded a fact of the course, and fixes two smaller things the same review found.

sections.heading: Scored, or complete or incomplete: said once
sections.body: When Folio outlines a course it now records, for each graded component, whether its work is scored or is graded complete or incomplete, as your brief says. Every page, assignment and rubric is told the same thing, along with what complete means (every rubric criterion at the second-highest level or above) and that the pieces of one component count equally unless you say otherwise. You can switch a component on the grading table of the syllabus.

image.alt: The grading table of the Unity sample: under each component, whether it is scored or complete or incomplete

sections.heading: A lesson that fails holds back the ones after it
sections.body: Folio writes each lesson from what the lessons before it hold. When one lesson could not be written, the build used to carry on, and week 13 was written without knowing week 12. Now the later lessons wait with it, and Resume writes them in order.

sections.heading: Optional means no deadline
sections.body: An optional reading used to keep “due Sunday night” on the week’s checklist, which read as required. Anything a page marks optional now has no due day.

title: Online courses: a page students follow alone, a live session that runs itself, or both
lede: A course taught online is not a classroom course on a screen. With no meetings, the week has to teach by itself; in a video meeting, nothing happens unless the plan names the tool. Folio now asks how the course is taught and writes it that way.

sections.heading: Say how the course is taught
sections.body: Beside the level and the number of lessons there is now a choice: in person, online in your own time, online live, or both. Folio also reads it from the brief (“asynchronous”, “on Zoom”, “one live session a week”). Each one is planned, written and checked by its own rules, which came from a review of what online course standards ask for.

image.alt: In person, own time, live, and both, with what Folio writes for each. The three online ways are new

sections.heading: A weekly page that teaches without you
sections.body: For a course with no set meeting time, each lesson is a week’s module page written to the student: why the week matters, a checklist with honest minutes and due days, the teaching in parts a student can finish in a sitting, checkpoints that say what they should now see, a “Stuck?” box with the likely causes, a self-check quiz, one forum prompt, and a wrap-up. Software courses become step-by-step tutorials with code blocks, and every picture and clip the page needs is specified for whoever makes it, with text for a student who cannot see it.

image.alt: Week 4 of the Unity sample: the checklist of the week with minutes for each item and the days things are due

sections.heading: Steps, code, pictures and files
sections.body: A week that teaches software is a tutorial: numbered steps with the exact names on screen, the code to type with each line explained, a picture after the step it belongs to, a checkpoint that says what you should now see, and the project files to download when something will not work. Each week is told what earlier weeks left in the student’s project, so week 5 does not put a ball where week 4 built a ramp.

image.alt: Week 2 of the Unity sample: numbered steps with a picture of the Inspector after the step that sets its values

sections.heading: Start here, and what only you can add
sections.body: Before week 1 students get a Start here page: what to do first, how a week runs, what to install, how the grade is made, where to ask. What only you can supply (your name and hours, late work, what help and AI tools are allowed, accommodations) is listed for you alone and never invented.

sections.heading: A live session is a run of show
sections.body: For a course taught in video meetings, the plan names the tool for every step: the prompt to paste in the chat on arrival, each poll with its options and what to do when most get it wrong, breakout task cards with roles and where the group writes, an exit ticket, and a fallback that needs only chat. No stretch of talk runs past fifteen minutes, long sessions get a break, and cameras are invited, never graded.

image.alt: A live session plan: an arrival prompt for the chat, with the instructor’s notes and a fallback

sections.heading: A sample you can open: fourteen weeks of Unity
sections.body: The new sample is an undergraduate course in game development for complete beginners, taught online in students’ own time. Every week was followed step by step in Unity 6.6 on a real machine: the code was compiled, the error messages checked word for word, and the pictures, clips and project files were made from that run. Week 12 was built three times, once for each route a student can take. Following it found things no reader could: a ball placed where an earlier week’s ramp still stood, white walls that hid a white score label, sparks too small to see from the camera. Then reviewers read it as a beginner would and as a department chair would. Where a mistake came from how Folio writes, the fix went into Folio, not only into the sample.

image.alt: Week 12 of the Unity sample: the steps for one route, with a picture of the level as it should look

sections.heading: More than one piece of graded work in a lesson
sections.body: A real syllabus sets a weekly response paper, a presentation and a term paper in the same week. A lesson can now hold several pieces, each with its own instructions, rubric and due lesson, and a standing piece (the same task every week) is written once and referred to after that.

title: Tests, presentations and answer keys: the graded work a real course runs on
lede: Until now Folio knew two kinds of work: an assignment done at home, and a step toward one. A midterm, an oral interview or a seminar a student leads had nowhere to live, so a paper worth 30% of a grade was a line in a lesson plan. This release gives all of it a place, with what a teacher needs to hand it out and grade it.

sections.heading: Four kinds of graded work
sections.body: When Folio outlines a course it now decides, for each lesson, what is handed in or graded there: an assignment, a step toward a larger piece, a test taken in class, or work graded in class with a rubric. Every component of the grade is placed in a lesson, and you can change any of them from the lesson itself.

image.alt: Assignment, step, test and in-class work, with what each one carries. Tests and in-class work are new

sections.heading: A test is a paper you can print
sections.body: A quiz, test or exam is written as the paper students are handed: the time allowed, what they may use, each question complete as printed, and the points it carries. It covers what the lessons taught in proportion to the time they took, with new cases and numbers. A final exam sat after the last class is written with the last lesson.

image.alt: A data structures midterm: two code fragments to analyze, each question with its points

compare.before: “Midterm exam (25%)” in the syllabus, and a lesson plan that said “students sit the midterm”.
compare.after: A paper with points for every question, a full key with the working, and the lesson plan that runs it.

sections.heading: Answer keys, for the teacher only
sections.body: Problem sets, labs and tests now come with an answer key: the answers with their working and what each point is for. The key is shown to you under the assignment and is never part of a student copy or a student export.

image.alt: The answer key under a programming exercise, marked “For you only: never in a student copy”

sections.heading: Work graded in class
sections.body: A presentation, a seminar a student leads, an oral interview or an essay written in class is now a piece of its own: what students prepare, a rubric, and how to run and score it for a whole class in the time you have. A piece that takes several days, or that students take turns at through the term, is written once and keeps one rubric.

image.alt: A graduate research methods course: seminar leadership, graded in class with a rubric

sections.heading: Due dates that agree
sections.body: Each assignment and step now has the lesson it is due at, set when the course is outlined. The lesson plan that sets the work, the assignment itself and the plan of the lesson that collects it all say the same thing.

compare.before: The plan said “due next week”, the assignment said “due Friday”, and the lesson two weeks on collected it.
compare.after: “Due at the start of lesson 4” on the assignment, and lesson 4 opens by collecting it.

sections.heading: For colleges and graduate schools
bullets: College rubrics in the United States and Canada use four levels (Exemplary, Proficient, Developing, Beginning) scored 4 to 1, so full marks can be earned.
Code is written out in full in the teacher’s notes, to run as it stands. In a data structures course we assembled and ran 62 blocks from the plans and both exam keys.

A graduate seminar is planned as a seminar: a student presents the reading and leads discussion, and the instructor presses on the argument. A doctoral seminar no longer starts with quizzes, slides, study guides and FAQs; turn any back on from the plan.

A case discussion is planned as a teaching note: the opening question, the discussion blocks in order, the board and the takeaway. When a brief promises cases and names none, Folio asks which you use, or writes short ones.
Class policies in your brief or syllabus (late work, attendance, integrity) are carried into the course in your words.
Readings are proposed for each lesson when you have not named them, marked as suggestions to check.

sections.heading: Also in this release
bullets: A meeting of two hours or more has a break in its plan.
“Twice a week” in a brief is read as two meetings, and “a computer lab” as a session of its own.
Participation that carries part of the grade gets a rubric and a way to record it.
Code in a lesson is no longer set with ligatures: “//=” was drawn as a not-equals sign.
A plan’s close announces a quiz only when there is one, and an exam does not repeat the items of the review before it.

title: Eight lessons means eight, and a few rules pulled back into line
lede: A short release. Re-reading the courses written after 0.0.3 showed that some of the new rules pushed too far. One of them changed the number of lessons you asked for, which is ours to fix at once.

sections.heading: The number of lessons you ask for is the number you get
sections.body: In 0.0.3 we told Folio to give a unit test most of a lesson. For a unit of eight lessons graded by a test, it made room by adding a ninth. The lessons you ask for now come first: the test is placed within them.

compare.before: You asked for eight 50-minute lessons. Folio planned nine.
compare.after: You asked for eight 50-minute lessons. Folio plans eight, with the test in the last.

sections.heading: A final exam is not forgotten
sections.body: Graded work is placed in lessons when the course is outlined. A final exam held in exam week, after the last class, belongs to no lesson, and a statistics course was written as if it had none. The last lesson now names the exam and reviews for it.

sections.heading: “Hypothetical”, once
sections.body: Folio labels invented examples so no one takes them for real studies. It was labelling them over and over, 104 times in one course, and once called a real dataset hypothetical. Now an invented example is marked once, where it is introduced, and real data is never marked.

compare.before: “In this hypothetical study of a hypothetical sample…” on seven of eleven worksheets, and on R’s real sleep data.
compare.after: “Suppose a survey of our school found…”, said once.

sections.heading: Also in this release
bullets: When a lesson holds a graded quiz, the lesson’s own quiz is that quiz and covers what the plan says it covers.
In a beginners’ language course, discussion prompts give instructions in English and sentence frames in the language being learned, not whole prompts in a language students cannot yet read.
Plans no longer mention handouts or files that the course does not have.

title: Seven sample courses, and courses with labs, code and languages
lede: Four more sample courses to explore, and fixes from check-ups of a ratios unit, a Spanish course and a statistics course taught with R. Two of them were plain bugs that would have broken a real class.

sections.heading: Seven sample courses, by stage
sections.body: The sample chooser now groups courses by stage, with four new ones. Like the first three, each was written by Folio from a teacher’s brief, then read lesson by lesson and corrected.
bullets: The water cycle, grade 5: five lessons built from a teacher’s own planning notes, with supports for struggling readers and a Spanish-speaking newcomer in every lesson.
Ratios and rates, grade 6: eight lessons with no homework, assessed by two in-class quizzes and a unit test with a full mark scheme.
Stoichiometry, grade 10: ten lessons with two labs, four problem sets with answer keys, and a unit test.
Reconstruction, 1865–1877, grade 11: eight lessons on named primary sources, a Socratic seminar and a document-based essay.

image.alt: The sample chooser with seven courses under elementary, middle, high school and university

sections.heading: A lab unit you could run
sections.body: The chemistry sample shows what the lab fixes add up to: quantities for a whole class, goggles, gloves and ventilation, a warning about the heat a reaction gives off, what to do for a splash in the eye, and how to dispose of the waste. The copper left to dry in one lesson is weighed in the next, and every problem set has new problems and an answer key.

image.alt: A chemistry lab lesson: predicting the limiting reactant before reacting aluminum with copper chloride

sections.heading: History from the documents
sections.body: The Reconstruction sample names every source students read, down to the passage, and tells you to prepare copies. Its essay lists the documents the unit actually used, its seminar has scoring a whole class can reach, and every exit ticket has its question and a simple score. Painful material comes with guidance: slurs are never read aloud, and no one plays a victim or an attacker.

image.alt: The map of the Reconstruction unit: eight lessons with plans, slides, study guides, quizzes and the essay

sections.heading: Code stays code
sections.body: Folio tidies quotation marks into curly ones. It was doing that inside code too, so every line of R with text in it failed when a student pasted it. Code is now left exactly as written. In our statistics course, 607 pieces of code, none changed.

sections.heading: “A lecture and a computer lab” is two meetings
sections.body: A brief that asked for “a 75-minute lecture and a 50-minute computer lab” each week got lectures only: the lab was missed because of the word “computer” in between. Folio now reads it as two meetings and plans both.

compare.before: Each week: one 75-minute lecture, with students somehow at computers.
compare.after: Each week: a 75-minute lecture and a 50-minute lab, each with its own plan.

sections.heading: A language course speaks the language
sections.body: Discussion prompts in a Spanish course were English debates about Spanish. They now get students using the language at their level. A lesson that teaches many words can also list all of them, not just eight.

compare.before: “A friend says, ‘Using usted is old-fashioned. We should just use tú with everyone.’ Do you agree?”
compare.after: “Imagina que tu compañero te pregunta: ¿Cómo estás? Hoy no te sientes ni bien ni mal. ¿Dices Regular o Bien?”

sections.heading: Also in this release
bullets: The class policies in your syllabus (late work, integrity, accommodations) are carried into the course.
A quiz or test has points for each question, enough time, and nothing left on the board that answers it.
A lesson’s graded quiz is the lesson’s own quiz, not a second set of questions.
The close of a lesson tells students what is coming next, including a quiz, and what to read.
A project due weeks after it is set asks for what the lessons up to then teach.
A weekly problem set repeats none of the last one’s problems.

title: A second read that changes the plan, and homework that is new work
lede: We wrote six more courses overnight, from grade 3 fractions to a college psychology course built from a syllabus, and had each one read lesson by lesson the way its teacher would. These are the fixes that came out of it.

sections.heading: When the second read finds a problem, the plan is rewritten
sections.body: Every lesson plan gets a second read before anything is built on it. Small fixes were made on the spot, but anything bigger used to be left as a note for you, while the slides, quiz and study guide were built on the flawed plan and repeated it. Now a plan left with notes is written once more, told what the read found, and read again. Whichever version comes out cleaner is kept. In our chemistry and history courses, the notes left for the teacher went from four each to none.

image.alt: Before, a review note stayed on an unchanged plan. Now the plan is rewritten with the note and read again

sections.heading: Homework is new work, not the class examples again
sections.body: Problem sets and quiz questions were being told to use the plan’s examples, so graded homework repeated what the class had just worked through together, with the answers already on the board. Now they keep the lesson’s methods and facts but give students new problems.

compare.before: In class: “6.0 mol H₂ makes how many mol NH₃?” For homework: “find the moles of NH₃ made from 6.0 mol H₂.”
compare.after: For homework: “For 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, write the mole ratio of Mg to MgO. Use it to find the moles of MgO made from 3.60 mol Mg.”

image.alt: A grade 10 chemistry problem set on mole ratios with new problems

sections.heading: Steps that build toward the big piece
sections.body: When several lessons set a step toward an essay or a paper, or a problem set every few days, each used to be written on its own. One course set the same step three lessons running. Now they are written in order, each knowing what the ones before asked, so steps build on each other and recurring work keeps one length and format. Homework also follows the rhythm you ask for: “twice a week” is twice a week, not every lesson.

image.alt: Before: the same step set three times. Now: an evidence log, a working claim, connecting evidence, then the essay

sections.heading: Tests have a lesson, questions, answers and points
sections.body: A unit test worth half the grade used to be only “previewed” in the last lesson. Now graded work that happens in class is given a lesson when the course is outlined, and a lesson with a test writes its questions, answer key and points out in full, asks about new cases, and keeps them out of that lesson’s study guide and quiz. The same goes for an exit ticket: its question and expected answer are in the plan. (A printable test paper as its own material is still to come.)

image.alt: The last lesson of a chemistry unit, now a 55-minute unit test with its rules and timing

sections.heading: Care with hard material, and with what students handle
sections.body: Plans now say how to handle painful content, and never ask students to play the people who suffered or inflicted it. Lab plans cover what a careful teacher would: protective gear, ventilation, the heat a reaction gives off, and disposal.

compare.before: “You are a returning Confederate soldier or a newly freed person in Georgia. What is the first problem you must solve?”
compare.after: “Violence is the content. Warn students before you begin, give plain facts without graphic detail, and let anyone step out quietly. Never assign roles of victims or attackers.”

sections.heading: Lessons hand over to each other
sections.body: A plan now knows what homework its own lesson sets and sets it before students leave; the next lesson collects or uses it. It knows what students should read before the next lesson and tells them. Later lessons see how earlier ones set things up, down to the teacher notes, and finish what was left for them, like a lab result waiting to be measured. Work that runs over several days is started early enough when the course is outlined.
bullets: Texts students read are named exactly, down to the passage, with a note to prepare copies; never just “an excerpt”.
A final essay asks only for what the course really gave students.
A paper for the whole course takes its topic from your brief, not from the lesson that happens to set it.
Slides show the items students work from, and hold back the answers until the reveal.
University courses say “instructor”, and keep any routine your syllabus asks for.

title: Sample courses, and courses that hold together
lede: Folio’s first numbered release. Three new sample courses to explore, and a round of improvements to how every course is written, found by building those samples to the standard of a teacher who has to teach them tomorrow.

sections.heading: Three sample courses, one for each stage
sections.body: “Or open a sample course” now lets you choose. Each one was written by Folio from a teacher’s brief, the same way your courses are, then read lesson by lesson and polished. Open one, change anything, export it: it is your own copy.
bullets: Elementary: plant and animal life cycles, a ten-lesson grade 2 science unit with a bean garden students watch grow.
Middle school: writing argumentative essays, a fifteen-lesson grade 8 unit built on two opinion articles about later school start times.
University: introduction to ethics, a fourteen-week semester with a lecture and a seminar every week.

image.alt: The sample chooser: elementary school, middle school and university

sections.heading: A full course at a glance
sections.body: Each sample is the size a teacher there would plan: a unit for school, a whole semester for university, with every lesson’s plan, slides, study guide, quiz, assignment, rubric, discussion questions and answers to students’ questions.

image.alt: The map of the fourteen-week ethics course, every lesson and its materials

sections.heading: Lessons that remember each other
sections.body: Lesson plans used to be written side by side, each knowing only the others’ titles, so one lesson could give a bean plant five stages and the next only four. Now each plan is written knowing what the lessons before it taught: the same terms and stages, the same cases, and anything still under way, like seeds sprouting by the window, carried on as it was set up. Each lesson lists only the vocabulary it introduces.

image.alt: Before: four lessons planned alone contradict each other. Now: each plan reads the ones before it

sections.heading: Plans you can teach as written
sections.body: Every plan now reads the way an experienced teacher would want it before walking into class.
bullets: Safety notes for anything students handle, taste, heat or cut, such as allergies or materials that must never be eaten.
Realistic timing for things that take days, counted against how often the class meets.
When a plan shows students how their work is scored, it uses the rubric’s own levels.
Slides shown during a test give its instructions only, never the answers.
Homework steps can be done at home, without a partner or classroom materials.
Other lessons are “last time” and “next time”, not quoted titles.

image.alt: A grade 2 lesson plan with key ideas, timed segments and teacher notes

sections.heading: Every material agrees with the plan
sections.body: Each plan gets a second read before anything is built on it. If the plan is written again, what that read found now goes into the rewrite, so the same mistake isn’t made twice. The reviewer also knows the slides, quiz and rubric are written separately, so it no longer asks for them inside the plan.

image.alt: Brief, outline, lesson plan, second read, and the materials written from the plan

sections.heading: Your files, cited by name
sections.body: When you attach articles or notes, Folio now refers to them by title or author, the way you would with students, never by internal passage numbers.

compare.before: The evidence is Torres’s report in passage [6] that students slept more.
compare.after: The evidence is Torres’s report that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.

sections.heading: Assessment that adds up
sections.body: When one graded piece is built across several lessons, each lesson now writes its own part, with its own title, instead of each claiming the whole grade. And when a course has weekly work as well as larger papers, every paper is set in a lesson, so none goes missing.

compare.before: Life cycle drawing and labeling check (“worth 100% of the course grade”) · Life cycle drawing and labeling check
compare.after: Life cycle drawing and labeling check: bean plant stage · Life cycle drawing and labeling check: butterfly and frog

sections.heading: How we find what to fix
sections.body: These improvements came from a new routine. We write real courses from teachers’ briefs, from grade 2 to university, check every part, and read each lesson as the teacher who would teach it. For every problem we ask why Folio wrote it and whether it would happen in another course. If it would, we fix the cause, so every teacher’s course gets better, not just the one we read.

image.alt: The quality routine: write real courses, check, read as a teacher, ask why, fix the cause, verify
